tips.title: Look for the OH on the end
tips.body: C₃H₇**OH** is an alcohol; C₃H₈ is an alkane and C₃H₆ an alkene. The shorthand is written to show the functional group, so recognising an alcohol from a formula is just spotting the OH written separately at the end.

tips.title: Ethanol has six hydrogens
tips.body: C₂H₅OH: five in the C₂H₅ and **one in the OH**. Forgetting that last hydrogen is the commonest way a combustion equation goes wrong, and it throws the water and then the oxygen out with it.

tips.title: The alcohol brings its own oxygen
tips.body: When balancing combustion, count the oxygen on the right, then subtract the **one** the alcohol already contains before working out how many O₂ molecules the air supplies. That single subtraction is the whole difficulty.

tips.title: Neutral, not acidic
tips.body: An alcohol dissolves in water to give a solution of about **pH 7**. The –OH looks acidic but does not release H⁺; it is the second oxygen in a **–COOH** that makes a carboxylic acid acidic.

tips.title: Anaerobic, or you make vinegar
tips.body: Fermentation needs **no oxygen** — with oxygen the ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid. And it needs 25–35 °C, because too hot **denatures** the enzymes and stops the reaction rather than speeding it up.

steps.title: The -OH group
steps.body:
An **alcohol** is a molecule containing the functional group **–OH**, a hydroxyl group.

The first four members of the homologous series are **methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol** — one, two, three and four carbons. These four names are the only ones you need.

They can be written in two ways, and both appear in exams:

- as a **shorthand**: CH₃OH, CH₃CH₂OH (often written C₂H₅OH), C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH
- as a **displayed formula**, with every bond drawn, including the O–H

Notice how the shorthand is written. Ethanol is C₂H₅OH rather than C₂H₆O, even though both count the same atoms, because writing the **OH separately shows the functional group**. A question that asks you to recognise an alcohol from a formula is asking you to spot that OH on the end.

The general formula is $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$.

steps.title: Four things alcohols do
steps.body:
The spec names four reactions of the first four alcohols, and you should be able to describe what happens in each.

**1. With sodium.** The alcohol **fizzes** and **hydrogen gas** is given off, leaving a solution. It is the same reaction sodium has with water, but **less vigorous**.

**2. Burning in air.** Alcohols burn readily with a **clean blue flame**, giving **carbon dioxide and water**. This is why they are used as fuels.

**3. Added to water.** The first four alcohols **dissolve completely**, and the solution is **neutral** — around pH 7. This matters: an alcohol is not an acid, whatever the OH might suggest.

**4. With an oxidising agent.** The alcohol is **oxidised to a carboxylic acid**. Ethanol becomes **ethanoic acid**, which is what happens when wine is left open and turns to vinegar.

That last one is worth holding on to, because it connects this topic to the next: alcohols are one step away from carboxylic acids.

steps.title: Burning an alcohol
steps.body:
Combustion is the **one** reaction of alcohols you are expected to write a balanced equation for, so it is worth being able to balance it rather than recall it.

The trick is the oxygen: the alcohol already contains **one oxygen atom**, so you need that one fewer from the air.

steps.title: Fermentation
steps.body:
Ethanol for drinks is not made from crude oil. It is made by **fermentation**: **yeast** converts a **sugar solution** into an **aqueous solution of ethanol** and carbon dioxide.

The conditions matter and are regularly asked for:

- a **sugar solution** in water — the yeast needs the sugar dissolved
- **yeast**, which supplies the enzymes
- a temperature of about **25 to 35 °C** — warm, but not hot
- **anaerobic** conditions: **no oxygen**, or the ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid instead

Why that temperature? Yeast works by **enzymes**. Too cold and the reaction is too slow to be useful; too hot and the enzymes **denature** and stop working altogether. So *warmer is faster* only up to a point, and then it fails completely — which is not how an ordinary reaction behaves.

Fermentation gives a **dilute, aqueous** solution of ethanol. The other industrial route — **hydration of ethene** with steam, from the previous topic — gives a much purer product and runs continuously, but needs crude oil as its raw material. Fermentation uses a **renewable** one.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the functional group of the alcohols and write the general formula.
2. Write the shorthand formula of propanol, and its molecular formula.
3. What is seen when sodium is added to ethanol, and what gas is given off?

**Part B.**

4. Balance the combustion of methanol: CH₃OH + ?O₂ → ?CO₂ + ?H₂O. Give whole-number coefficients.
5. State the four conditions needed for fermentation.
6. Ethanol is added to water. What is the pH of the solution, and why?

**Part C.**

7. Compare fermentation with the hydration of ethene as ways of making ethanol. Give two advantages of each.
8. Explain why fermentation stops working if the temperature is raised well above 35 °C, and why this is different from an ordinary reaction getting faster when heated.

For question 4, remember the methanol brings its own oxygen atom to the left-hand side.

steps.title: Going deeper: what the -OH does and does not do
steps.body:
**An alcohol is neutral, not acidic.** This catches people, because –OH looks like the OH⁻ of an alkali and because the next topic's acids also contain an O–H. But a solution of ethanol has a pH of about **7**. The O–H bond in an alcohol does not release a hydrogen ion into water in any appreciable amount.

What makes a carboxylic acid acidic is the **whole –COOH group**: the second oxygen, double-bonded to the same carbon, pulls electrons away and makes the O–H bond much easier to break. So it is not the O–H alone but its surroundings — which is a good example of the general rule that in organic chemistry the **functional group**, not the individual atom, decides the behaviour.

**Why alcohols dissolve in water and alkanes do not.** The –OH group can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so the small alcohols mix with water completely. Alkanes have no such group and do not. As the carbon chain gets longer, the hydrocarbon part starts to dominate and solubility falls — which is why the spec names the **first four** alcohols.

**Two routes to ethanol, and the argument between them.** Fermentation uses a **renewable** raw material and mild conditions, but works in **batches**, is **slow**, and gives a **dilute aqueous** product that needs distilling. Hydration of ethene is **fast**, **continuous** and gives **pure** ethanol, but needs **crude oil**, which is finite, and **high temperature and pressure**, which costs energy. A question asking you to *evaluate* wants both sides and then a judgement — and the judgement usually turns on whether the raw material or the purity matters more for the use.

**One equation only.** You are expected to balance **combustion** and nothing else in this topic. For sodium, water and oxidation, describe what happens and name the products — that is what carries the marks.

**Watch the hydrogen count.** In C₂H₅OH there are **six** hydrogens, not five: five in the C₂H₅ and one in the OH. Missing that hydrogen is the commonest way a combustion equation goes wrong.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **alcohol** has the functional group **–OH**; general formula $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$.
- The first four are **methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol**.
- Ethanol is written **C₂H₅OH** rather than C₂H₆O, because that shows the functional group.
- **With sodium**: fizzes, giving **hydrogen** — like water but less vigorous.
- **Burning**: a clean flame giving carbon dioxide and water. $C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O$.
- **In water**: dissolves completely, and the solution is **neutral**, about pH 7.
- **With an oxidising agent**: oxidised to a **carboxylic acid** — ethanol to ethanoic acid.
- **Uses**: fuels and solvents, and ethanol in drinks.
- **Fermentation**: sugar solution, yeast, **25 to 35 °C**, **anaerobic**.
- Too hot and the enzymes **denature**, so the reaction stops rather than speeds up.
- Fermentation is **renewable but slow and dilute**; hydration of ethene is **fast and pure but needs crude oil**.
- Only **combustion** needs a balanced equation; and C₂H₅OH has **six** hydrogens.

questions.prompt: Ethanol can be made by fermentation or by the hydration of ethene. Compare the two processes, giving the conditions each needs, and evaluate which is the better way to make ethanol.
questions.solution: Fermentation uses a solution of sugar with yeast added, kept at about twenty five to thirty five degrees Celsius in anaerobic conditions, meaning without oxygen. The raw material is sugar from plants, which is renewable, and the conditions are mild so little energy is needed. However, fermentation is slow, it is carried out in batches rather than continuously, and it produces a dilute aqueous solution of ethanol which must then be distilled. Hydration of ethene uses steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst at about three hundred degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres pressure. It is fast, runs continuously and produces pure ethanol, but the ethene comes from crude oil, which is a finite resource, and the high temperature and pressure require a great deal of energy. Which is better depends on the purpose. For alcoholic drinks only fermentation can be used because the raw material must be food. For an industrial solvent where purity and a continuous supply matter, hydration of ethene is better, although as crude oil becomes scarcer the renewable route becomes more attractive.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Fermentation.** Sugar solution, yeast, about **25 to 35 °C**, **anaerobic**.

- **For:** a **renewable** raw material (sugar from plants), and mild conditions using little energy.
- **Against:** **slow**, run in **batches**, and gives a **dilute aqueous** solution that must be distilled.

**Hydration of ethene.** Steam, **phosphoric acid catalyst**, about **300 °C**, **60 to 70 atmospheres**.

- **For:** **fast**, **continuous**, and gives **pure** ethanol.
- **Against:** ethene comes from **crude oil**, which is finite, and the conditions cost a great deal of energy.

**The judgement.** It depends on the use, and saying so is the mark:

- For **drinks**, fermentation is the only possibility — the raw material has to be food.
- For an **industrial solvent**, hydration wins on purity and continuous supply.
- As crude oil becomes scarcer, the renewable route becomes more attractive whatever the use.

An answer that simply declares one better without naming what it is better *for* does not get the final mark.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens when ethanol reacts with sodium, when it burns in air, when it is added to water, and when it is treated with an oxidising agent. Give a balanced equation for the combustion.
questions.solution: When sodium is added to ethanol the mixture fizzes and hydrogen gas is given off, leaving a solution. The reaction is similar to that of sodium with water but less vigorous. When ethanol burns in air it burns readily with a clean blue flame, producing carbon dioxide and water. The balanced equation is C two H five O H plus three O two goes to two C O two plus three H two O. When ethanol is added to water it dissolves completely and the resulting solution is neutral, with a pH of about seven, showing that an alcohol is not an acid. When ethanol is treated with an oxidising agent it is oxidised to ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid with the same two carbon atoms, which is the same change that occurs slowly when wine is left open to the air and turns into vinegar.

questions.modelAnswer:
**With sodium.** The mixture **fizzes** and **hydrogen** is given off, leaving a solution. It is the same reaction as sodium with water, but **less vigorous**.

**Burning in air.** A clean flame, giving **carbon dioxide and water**:

$$C_2H_5OH + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O$$

Check it: C 2 = 2, H 6 = 6, O 1 + 6 = 4 + 3 ✓. The ethanol's own oxygen counts on the left, and there are **six** hydrogens, not five.

**Added to water.** It **dissolves completely**, and the solution is **neutral** — about pH 7. Despite the O–H, an alcohol is not an acid.

**With an oxidising agent.** Oxidised to **ethanoic acid**, a carboxylic acid with the same two carbons. This is what happens slowly to wine left open to the air.

Only the combustion needs an equation; the other three are described.

examTechnique.body:
Recognise an alcohol by the OH written at the end of the formula, and say which of the first four it is by counting carbons.

For the four reactions, describe what is seen as well as what is formed: fizzing with sodium, a clean flame when burning, dissolving to a neutral solution, and oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

Only combustion needs a balanced equation. Count the hydrogen in the OH, and remember the alcohol supplies one oxygen atom of its own.

For fermentation, give all four conditions. Questions often want the reason as well: anaerobic because oxygen would oxidise the ethanol, and 25 to 35 °C because the enzymes denature above that.

When comparing fermentation with hydration of ethene, give points on both sides and then a judgement tied to the use.
examinerErrors: Saying an alcohol solution is acidic because it contains an O-H bond.
Counting five hydrogens in C2H5OH instead of six.
Forgetting that the alcohol supplies one oxygen atom when balancing combustion.
Giving the conditions for hydration of ethene when asked about fermentation.
Leaving out anaerobic from the conditions for fermentation.
Saying fermentation gives pure ethanol, when the product is dilute and aqueous.
Writing a balanced equation for the reaction with sodium, which is not required and is usually wrong.
Naming the product of oxidation as an aldehyde or an alkene rather than a carboxylic acid.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer separates what is seen from what is formed, so a description of the sodium reaction has fizzing in it as well as hydrogen. It balances combustion by counting oxygen on the right and subtracting the one the alcohol brought, rather than by trial. It explains why an alcohol is neutral in terms of the O–H not releasing hydrogen ions, and can then say what is different about –COOH. On fermentation it gives reasons with the conditions, and knows that heating past 35 °C stops the reaction rather than speeding it up, because enzymes denature. Comparing the two industrial routes, it reaches a judgement tied to the use rather than declaring one simply better.
